Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
I dwell on how I used to be before the event
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
I have lost my connection to my community and culture
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Exercise: Exercise' is not clinically well aligned with the rest of the profile. The other selected strategies are cognitive perseveration focused on the trauma and pre-trauma self, while the threat and memory items emphasize hypervigilance, nighttime fear, and fragmented sensory/emotional memory. Avoiding exercise addresses a different symptom domain and, given the formulation, is hard to connect plausibly to the active Memory/Threat/Negative Appraisals pathways driving maladaptive strategies.

vignette:
Zara commands a vessel the length of three football fields, guiding thousands of tons of steel and cargo through treacherous seas with an authority that is absolute. At 53, she is a master of her domain, respected for her calm under pressure. But the moment she steps across the threshold of her own home, that authority dissolves. The quiet, carpeted hallways of her house feel more menacing to her than any storm on the Atlantic. The trauma did not happen at sea; it happened in a bedroom that looked much like this one, four decades ago, at the hands of a relative entrusted with her care.

The memories of that time rarely arrive as a coherent story. More often, they are fragments. Sometimes, while sitting with her husband watching television, a profound and sickening dread will rise in her chest, a full-body echo of childhood terror so intense she has to grip the arms of her chair, yet there is no picture in her mind to accompany it. On other occasions, when asked about her childhood, she can recount certain events with a chilling detachment, her voice flat as if narrating a stranger’s biography, feeling nothing at all. Then there are the images: sudden, intrusive flashes of the floral wallpaper in her old room, the shape of a shadow falling across the door, the specific glint of a belt buckle. These visual intrusions are silent but potent, capable of hijacking her entire sense of reality in a split second.

Over the years, Zara has come to believe that the world is an inherently unsafe place, a conviction forged in the silence of the adults who should have noticed, who should have protected her. In her mind, their failure was a betrayal as profound as the abuse itself, severing her connection not just to her family, but to the community and culture they represented. She feels like an outsider at family gatherings, the warmth and laughter a painful reminder of a belonging she can never reclaim. This sense of fundamental danger follows her home from every voyage. She cannot relax, even with her husband beside her. Every creak of the floorboards, every rustle of leaves outside the window is a potential intruder. Night is the worst. She finds herself lying awake for hours, straining to hear any sound that might signal someone entering the house, her body rigid with a vigilance that never fully subsides.

Her days on shore are consumed by a quiet, internal battle. She spends hours dwelling on a past she cannot change, caught in torturous loops of how it all could have been prevented. If only she had screamed louder. If only her mother hadn't trusted him. If only she had been a different child. This rumination alternates with a deep, aching grief for the person she was before, the woman who could feel safe in her own home. She tries to suppress the thoughts, to build a wall in her mind, but it is an exhausting and futile effort. The harder she pushes, the more violently the memories and feelings break through. Her husband sees the toll it takes—the distance in her eyes, the way she flinches at his touch if she is not expecting it. He feels her slipping away into a place he cannot reach. It was after he found her, frozen in the hallway at 3 a.m., staring at the front door, that they agreed she needed to seek help. Zara is terrified of dredging up the past, but the hope of one day feeling the same peace in her home that she feels on the open ocean is, for the first time, stronger than her fear.
